I've been farming these same fields for 50 years, so I know what each plot can give me. With high school behind me, I read the fertilizer bags carefully and I talk to the agro-technicians when they come through the village. But in the end, I trust what I've seen work on my own land.

My 9 mu splits into two parts. I put 5 mu into the wheat-maize rotation — that's the backbone, two harvests a year, and the well water reaches those plots easily. The other 4 mu I keep in cotton because the soil there is a bit saltier and cotton tolerates it better than grain. I've done it this way for over a decade.

For winter wheat, I sow improved Jimai variety around October 10. I base-apply about 40 kg of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) per mu before plowing, then topdress 15 kg of urea per mu at jointing in spring. That gives me roughly 20 kg N, 8 kg P, 6 kg K per mu. I irrigate four times — before winter, at jointing, at heading, and at grain filling. Last year I got 480 kg/mu and I expect similar. Two sprays handle aphids and powdery mildew.

For summer maize, right after wheat harvest in June I direct-seed Zhengdan hybrid without tilling — no time to plow, and the stubble holds moisture. I side-dress urea at knee-high and again at tasseling, total about 18 kg N per mu, plus 6 kg P and 6 kg K from a base compound. Two irrigations usually — at the big trumpet stage and grain filling — unless rain comes. I target 600 kg/mu.

For cotton, I plough deep in spring, apply base compound giving 15 kg N, 7 kg P, 8 kg K per mu. I know cotton needs more potassium than grain. I irrigate three times through the season. Cotton takes the most spraying — five rounds for bollworm, aphids, and spider mites. I expect about 260 kg/mu of seed cotton.

I don't chase the highest yields — at my age I want steady returns and I don't want to pour money into extra fertilizer that just runs off.
